articles.title: Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
articles.summary: Signal is limiting users' ability to take screenshots in both its Android and iOS apps.
articles.content:
In Brief
Posted:
1:37 PM PST · November 21, 2026
Image Credits:
Matthias Balk/picture alliance / Getty Images
Anthony Ha
Signal restricts mobile screenshots as it confronts ‘existential threat’ of AI surveillance
Signal
announced Friday
that it’s limiting users’ ability to take screenshots within the secure messaging app — a response to what
President Meredith Whittaker
described as the “existential threat” of operating systems that integrate agentic AI.
Whittaker wrote that by giving AI agents the ability to “scan” the information on users’ screens, Windows, Android, and macOS/iOS “are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy.”
“Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment,” she said. “All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.”
Signal already sought to limit these risks by blocking screenshots of its Windows app by default. Now it’s adding similar restrictions in Android and iOS.
That said, users can disable this setting if they wish, which Whittaker said would “break our privacy guarantees.” She also admitted this is an “incomplete” solution, as it doesn’t “address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data.”

articles.title: A tale of two Nvidias
articles.summary: We got two very different pictures of Nvidia —  the company’s latest earnings report vs. the tech executives loudly calling for Jensen Huang’s return.
articles.content:
Listen on
Apple Podcasts
Listen on
Spotify
We got two very different pictures of Nvidia this week, depending on whether you were focused on the company’s latest earnings report or the tech executives loudly calling for former CEO Jensen Huang’s return.
On the latest episode of
TechCrunch’s Equity podcast
, Kirsten Korosec, Tim De Chant, and I discussed the latest news from the AI chipmaker,
which reported soaring revenue
and insisted that it has no plans for Huang to return.
Kirsten described this as “the tale of two Nvidias this week,” with the company’s current executives assuring investors, “Hey, we’ve got this.” At the same time, “You’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really
pushing to bring Jensen back
, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back.” (The company’s falling stock price certainly suggests that Wall Street isn’t feeling reassured.)
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity.
Kirsten Korosec:
Nvidia will no longer sell its H200 chips in China
. This was coming directly from the interim CEO Colette Kress, and that coincides with the Trump administration also talking about closing off what we have discussed in the past, which is this idea of remote access — really closing and tightening all these restrictions [so] the chips can’t make it into China.
What was happening is that data centers were being set up right outside, in countries like Malaysia and elsewhere, and then companies within China were remote accessing these chips, and so that’s now also been shut down.
A lot is happening on the China front that is so much bigger than Nvidia, but Nvidia came out publicly and said, “Nope, we’re shutting this part down.” I’ll be very curious to see if this changes, maybe in the first half of 2027.
Tim De Chant:
I’d love to be a fly on the wall in some of these Trump administration conversations, because they were much more stringent in terms of export controls at the end of the first Trump administration, and that continued through the Biden administration, where they really restricted Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China. I think that something changed in the last couple of years that really opened Nvidia’s ability to sell in the country.
Anthony Ha:
One of the things that really surprised me as we were preparing for this episode was [learning that critics] of Nvidia’s stance towards China estimate that 20% of their business comes from China.
And again, that’s not something you’re going to see directly in their financials, because that’s not direct sales to Chinese companies. But they’re saying, “A lot of the chips that are getting sold to companies in Malaysia or other companies in East Asia or Southeast Asia are going to end up [used by companies in] China eventually.” And so that could be —
if
Nvidia is really serious about this, I think this is something that’s very much in flux — that could actually be a pretty significant blow to their bottom line.
Kirsten:
Although Nvidia’s bottom line is doing just fine. In every possible way, their guidance was incredible. They beat expectations. They have a long pipeline.
It was really interesting because you have that happening, and then you have all this noise happening in social media, and also a number of other tech conferences were happening this past week — Dealbook Summit, there [were] a few others in which you had the highest profile people that you can think of in the tech world commenting on Jensen [Huang], and Jensen himself commenting.
So it’s like the tale of two Nvidias this week. You’ve got the earnings and the current executives really talking about, “Hey, we’ve got this.” In fact, that was the last line that Collette Kress said [on the earnings call]. And then at the exact same time, or in parallel, you’ve got Elon Musk and others out there really pushing to bring Jensen back, circulating a petition, Jensen himself saying that he’s prepared to come back. So it’s really quite the drama that we are definitely not done with, by the way.
Anthony:
Although I think that what the folks who’d like to see Jensen Huang come back would say is that this most recent quarter is the last quarter under him. This is the [last of the] good times that we’re seeing under him. And so we don’t know how well Nvidia will do without him.
It seems like Nvidia’s public stance right now [on Huang’s possible return] is, “No, that’s not happening.” But Nvidia’s public stance a week and a half before that was, “We stand behind Jensen. We have every confidence in his leadership.”
So depending on the various pressures on them, you can imagine that changing. I don’t know what it would take for that to happen. I don’t necessarily think it’s that likely, but I also don’t think that just because they’re saying it’s not happening
now
doesn’t mean it will
never
happen.
Kirsten:
Sure, never say never.
Tim:
Right, never say never. I do think that to some extent, their steadfastness and how quickly they shot down the petitions asking for Jensen to return suggests there’s maybe a little bit more going on behind the scenes than we know on the outside. So that’s probably something to watch in the coming weeks.
Kirsten:
I think that the board is trying to be in control here, and they don’t want to be forced into a decision because someone like Elon Musk is saying that it needs to happen. And so, even if there is a day in which Jensen returns — which I think is pretty unlikely, especially because the investigation into how much and who knew what about chips being sold, allegedly, secretly to China. We don’t know the full picture of that yet. But even if they did have the full picture, they want to present control, and they definitely don’t want to appear like they have deference to some other tech billionaire out there.
Tim:
I’m sure they’re looking at what happened at OpenAI and not wanting to repeat that.
Anthony:
I imagine the dynamic’s a little bit different, since Nvidia is a public company. So, I’m not an expert on this, but I would guess it would be much harder for you Jensen Huang to come back and just toss out a bunch of board members.

articles.title: Here are the top AI agents that can live in your text messages
articles.summary: We created a list of the most notable AI agents that can live in your text messages, from general assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
articles.content:
Rather than downloading another app, a growing number of agents can simply be texted like an ordinary person.
You text it what you need, and it can remember context, connect to the apps and services you already use, and complete tasks on your behalf. That can mean scheduling an appointment, organizing a calendar, researching a trip, sending an email, making a reservation, shopping online, or reminding you about something days later.
While Instinct is one of the buzziest AI agents at present,
thanks to its $10 billion valuation after its latest funding round
of $1 billion, there are many others also making a play for this space.
Below are the most notable options so far, from general-purpose personal assistants to agents designed for families, travel, and work.
Ask Proxy
Image Credits:
Ask Proxy
Ask Proxy
’s biggest differentiator is that it “thinks like a woman,” meaning it aims to anticipate your needs before you even ask, the company explains on its website.
It works like a chatbot you can text like a friend, whether you need gift ideas, help planning an event, or recommendations for things to do that weekend. You can ask it to add important dates to your calendar, set reminders, or help with everyday decisions. You can also send it photos, like an empty table, to figure out how to decorate the table for a dinner party.
Unlike a typical chatbot, Ask Proxy also takes a proactive approach. It can reach out when it notices something you might forget or when it comes across a new activity, restaurant, or experience you might enjoy.
There’s also a work-focused version, which the company explains “gets employees back to work faster, while keeping personal data off company systems.”
The personal version costs $1 per day. For businesses, pricing starts at $15 per employee per month for large companies and $23 per employee per month for small teams with fewer than 49 employees.
Ask Proxy works over SMS. You can text “start” to 820-732-2625.
Caddy
Image Credits:
Caddy
Caddy
is an AI assistant that turns the information scattered across your phone into things you can actually act on. It lives in iMessage for iPhone users and RCS for Android users, so there’s no separate app or inbox to constantly check.
For instance, an email contains an appointment that needs to be added to your calendar or a friend sends a list of things to pick up. Instead of worrying about all the details getting buried, Caddy connects to your calendars and conversations, then identifies things that may require action. It can add events to your calendar, set reminders, keep track of follow-ups, and even do research for you.
Caddy has been available in public beta since April 2026.
Comma
Image Credits:
Comma
Comma
is designed to manage tasks across both work and everyday life. Comma carries tasks through to completion, checking its own work and determining when a task is finished.
Completed work is surfaced for review when a decision or approval is needed. It also proactively notifies users and recommends the next steps.
It can work across a user’s browser, computer, and files, while remaining accessible remotely through messaging apps such as Signal, Telegram, and WeChat. Comma maintains context and memory across devices and conversations, and can deliver daily briefings, flag urgent matters, and summarize recorded calls.
Comma is free to start and open source.
Fambot
Image Credits:
Fambot
Fambot
is an AI-powered “chief of staff” for families, designed to bring together the many moving parts of family life, including school communications, sports activities, meal planning, calendars, and other day-to-day responsibilities, and turn them into an organized plan.
The service is designed to work across both an app and text messages. Fambot is available on iOS devices, Android devices, and the web, and families can also interact with it directly over SMS. Every night, Fambot automatically sends a summary of the following day, including upcoming events, to-dos, and details such as school uniform or packing requirements. Parents can reply to those messages to ask questions, check information, or make changes to their calendar.
Fambot currently connects to Gmail, Google Calendar, Outlook, and WhatsApp, with support for Apple Calendar planned for the future.
The company
launched
in beta in early September 2026 and has raised $3.5 million in pre-seed funding. The service is currently free during the beta period, but Fambot expects to eventually charge roughly the equivalent of a Netflix subscription.
Folk
Image Credits:
Folk
Folk
is designed to be an AI assistant you can reach through iMessage, WhatsApp, and Telegram. It can remember personal context, manage reminders, research topics, track flights, handle email, and perform real-world tasks such as restaurant reservations.
One distinction is that Folk runs on its own private cloud computer. It can also run code and execute multi-step tasks rather than merely responding conversationally.
Folk launched its beta in May 2026, and it’s available for free but also offers a Pro subscription for $8.33/month if you want unlimited tasks running in the background.
Haven
Image Credits:
Haven
Haven
distinguishes itself by presenting the concept of a “digital twin” rather than merely serving as a text-based AI assistant.
According to the company, Haven understands and adapts to your preferences, routines, and decision-making styles, creating a personalized memory graph based on your interactions. As the company
describes
, “A personal assistant knows what you asked it to do. Haven knows what you would do and how you would do it.”
Notably, the company envisions future features that customize your experiences across devices, like TV and car.
Currently, Haven is available for free in beta on iPhone and Android devices, and the web. You can also reach Haven by calling or texting (435) 260-6500.
Instinct
Image Credits:
Instinct
Instinct
first made headlines after raising
$350 million
at a $2.5 billion valuation. In September 2026, it raised
$1 billion
, valuing it at $10 billion.
The always-available agent can take actions on your behalf, rather than simply answer questions. Users can communicate with Instinct by text or voice and connect it to the apps and services they already use, such as email, calendar, Google Workspace, and more. The company says early users have used Instinct for tasks ranging from planning trips and buying groceries to booking tickets and canceling subscriptions.
In September, Instinct began giving users
dedicated email addresses
for their assistants. The idea is to let Instinct create and manage accounts on a user’s behalf without filling the user’s personal inbox. The agent can use its address to sign up for services, contact businesses, follow up on requests, and handle tasks that require an email account. (However, this level of autonomy has also raised concerns about
privacy and security
.) It’s also begun
rolling out support for placing calls
.
The company remains in private beta.
Iris
Image Credits:
Iris
Powered by Hermes Agent,
Iris
is designed to let users delegate tasks to an AI assistant directly through iMessage. Users can connect the apps they use and hand over a task with a simple message. The agent then works through the required steps, while retaining relevant context from previous interactions. It’s also designed to follow up with users proactively rather than waiting for another request.
Martin
Image Credits:
Martin
Martin
is a general-purpose personal assistant reachable through SMS as well as phone, WhatsApp, email, Slack, and its own
iOS
app.
It can help manage calendars, email, reminders, tasks, notes, and communications. It can also act on behalf of users by sending messages or making phone calls, while providing daily summaries of what needs attention.
It’s a bit on the pricier side, with subscriptions starting at $21 per month.
Maverick
Image Credits:
Maverick
Maverick
describes itself as an “AI companion who lives in your texts,” acting as a personal assistant that helps manage everyday tasks directly from your messages.
It can fix typos, cancel subscriptions, schedule meetings from voice notes, and help group chats settle on a date for an event. One notable feature is that Maverick asks for your permission before taking action.
The platform also offers hundreds of integrations, including Discord, Gmail, and Slack, allowing it to connect with the apps you already use.
It’s currently in beta and free to use on iMessage. There’s also a Pro version for €27 per month (or approximately $30.25 USD), which includes 500 tasks a month,  20 connected apps, scheduled tasks, and memory.
Miso
Image Credits:
Miso
Miso
takes the personal-assistant concept and applies it specifically to travel.
It operates through iMessage and combines AI trip planning with support from a dedicated travel team. Users can arrange flights through messaging while Miso takes into account their travel preferences, loyalty points, and other priorities. Miso also gives travelers access to trip details and flight updates, along with personalized recommendations.
Ohai
Image Credits:
Ohai
Ohai
is another family assistant focused on helping households manage the constant stream of information and tasks involved in everyday family life.
Users can send messages, forward emails, or make voice requests, and the assistant can transform them into schedules, reminders, and plans. It can also coordinate calendars, household chores, and meals across multiple members of a family.
It includes a free basic option, but also offers different subscriptions based on family size, starting at $9.99 per month.
Orbits
Image Credits:
Orbits
Orbits
also has an AI assistant that is focused on the household.
It works through both the Orbits app and text messaging, and can bring together calendars, lists, and conversations while also carrying out tasks for you. That can include searching the web, making purchases, booking restaurants, changing appointments, and requesting quotes for household services.
Additionally, Orbits can remind family members about chores, communicate with service providers, and help coordinate responsibilities beyond the immediate household.
Orbits is backed by investors like Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) Speedrun fund, N49P, and Garage Capital.
Pally
Image Credits:
Pally
Users can interact with
Pally
as they would with a friend while giving it access to the apps they already rely on. The assistant can connect information spread across services such as WhatsApp, Gmail, calendars, and Google Drive, helping users keep track of plans, receipts, dates, files, and other details.
There’s a free plan available. It works over iMessage, RCS, and Telegram.
Poke
Image Credits:
Poke/The Interaction Company of California
Poke
launched
in March 2026 as a general-purpose assistant that you can reach through text messaging. It can handle tasks involving calendars, planning, health and fitness, smart-home controls, photos, and other everyday activities.
Poke became particularly notable in June 2026 when Apple
approved
Poke as the first AI agent on the Apple Messages for Business platform. A month later, parent company The Interaction Company of California was
acquired
by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valued in the low nine figures.
Rene
Image Credits:
Rene
Rene
is an AI personal assistant designed to be a user’s “best contact” rather than another productivity agent. It’s text-based and can turn natural-language conversations into tasks, reminders, summaries, and other follow-up actions. Rene also maintains context across conversations, allowing it to remember details and surface things that may need attention later.
Additionally, it has a browser, can write code, shop for you, as well as create slides and images.
Rene is currently available on iMessage, Telegram, and WhatsApp.

Skye

agentic homescreen

articles.title: Is selling an AI version of your face to this microdrama startup the future of Hollywood?
articles.summary: An actor has licensed his face to a microdrama startup — in a trend that's already popular in China. Experts question the long-term consequences if this becomes a trend in Hollywood, too.
articles.content:
For the most part, the content offered by the microdrama startup Shortical is indistinguishable from
the rest of its industry
. The company produces soapy, melodramatic storylines — almost always risqué romances — that, in bite-sized two-minute episodes, compel viewers to stay glued to their phones so as not to miss the latest twist in a tawdry, cliff-hanger-happy saga.
The primary way that Shortical — which was founded last January — makes money is through subscriptions. Typically, the first 7-10 episodes of a micro-drama are free. After that, if the user wants to finish the series, they have to pay a small monthly fee which unlocks access to all of the site’s content.
Over the past year, the company has churned out a gush of popular live-action romances like “Crossing the Line with My Neighbor,” “Accidentally Married My Boss,” and “Spoiled by My Billionaire Sugar Daddy.”
Lately, however, the company’s homepage is covered in AI-generated content. The reason isn’t exactly hard to figure out: the production overhead for AI content is substantially less than live-action. The profit potential, meanwhile, is substantially higher, if you can draw an audience.
Its latest microdrama premiered in Los Angeles last week. The series, called “Inevitable,” stars Aki Avni, an Israeli film and television star who has been visible in American TV shows for years (he had a stint on Fox’s 9/11-era thriller “24” years ago) but is now trying something largely unheard of in modern Hollywood: licensing his face to Shortical for the sake of its AI content.
The project, which is wholly AI, used Avni’s face to create a digital avatar of him. In “Inevitable,” he plays himself – in a very meta plot in which he — the actor Aki Avni — licenses his face to a film studio, after which thriller-like antics ensue.
This is Shortical’s first foray into such a licensing deal, but it likely won’t be their last.
In a phone interview, Avni told TechCrunch that he found the project both nerveracking and exciting. “Look, it’s a new era for artists,” the actor said. “AI is a new kind of art. It’s a new format. It’s always great to be the pioneer in something.”
Guy Shimoni, the CEO of Shortical, emphasized the creative potential of the new tool. “One of the things that AI does is it enables smaller teams to be able to produce these movie-scale productions,” Shimoni said. “When we were doing mobile-first live action, we were limited by budget, but now we can serve them with epic fantasies. We have kingdoms and dragons. We have superheroes. We have werewolves.”
But AI-generated romances involving werewolves — who, exactly, is watching this kind of thing?
Apparently, a lot of people. While China
boasts the biggest microdrama audience
globally, Shimoni says that most of his platform’s viewers are actually in the U.S. The industry’s viewer demographic
skews heavily female
. Many viewers may watch them
to wind down at night
, getting minor dopamine hits as they drift off to sleep. Many of the AI-generated programs that already exist on the company’s website appear to have millions of views.
Now, Shortical is betting on the creation of a new generation of creators — those who, like Avni, are willing to surrender their likenesses for compensation. “
LICENSE YOUR FACE
” Shortical’s website advertises, explaining that interested parties can submit their social media handles to the company, which will then decide whether to offer them “a contract setting out the terms” of using their persona in the company’s AI-generated content.
A company rep told TechCrunch that this “offering is still in its early days and hasn’t yet resulted in any signed contracts.” They added: “The series with Aki is the first time Shortical has used a real person’s likeness, and it was done through a direct agreement with him rather than through the platform. Shortical hopes the series will draw more attention to face licensing and plans to promote the offering more actively following this launch.”
Much of this trend has
already taken hold in China
where the microdrama industry originated, where AI-generated content is big, and where face-licensing is already a trend. Although the trend may not be a particularly profitable one for creators. A
recent report
in Rest of World found that Microdrama firms were paying people “between US$15 to US$700 to license their facial likenesses.”
How much money is Shortical offering for its face-licensing deals? The company isn’t saying. As for if Shortical will offer royalty-based compensation for creators — like the residual system in television, “It’s a case by case [basis],” Shimoni answers vaguely.
A Shortical representative further explained to TechCrunch that the company didn’t want to “share a specific figure” for Avni’s particular contract. However, the person said, he came “on as a partner in the project, and his compensation was in line with industry standards for a comparable non-AI acting role.”
For other actors, however, the deals may be quite different. Plus, many creatives are understandably unsettled by signs of automation creeping into their industry. Until recently, microdramas seemed like a safe, entry-level gateway into the entertainment industry, where young actors could gain experience on sets and hone their craft. Now, companies are downsizing and producing content that doesn’t even require real actors.
Jennifer Cooper, a longtime fan of the industry and founder of the consultancy firm Vertical Drama Love, notes that there’s a lot of distrust of AI — both from audiences and within the microdrama industry itself.
“Everyone’s been impacted by AI,” she said. “A lot of us have either lost work to AI or can see that it’s devastated this industry — [taking microdramas] from something that was a rare thing in the world, that was in growth, and providing work, particularly for young people…[and now] you know, it’s been decimated.”
Questions of consent with AI likenesses have also dogged the industry (some creators
claim they have had their likenesses stolen
), which is something that Shortical is obviously trying to address with its new face-licensing endeavor.
Yet these licensing deals could also help to gig-ify the industry, creating a scenario in which creators pay a distributor for the chance to platform their content (or their face), then receive payouts based on the audience engagement they’re allowed to generate. Shortical
recently partnered
with a company called Payouts.com, which describes itself as a “payout infrastructure platform powering creator and gig economy disbursements at scale.” The plan is to create a system by which creatives can seamlessly interact with Shortical’s platform and get paid.
Cooper believes the push towards AI in the industry is driven by broader financial trends. Most of the microdrama business is led by startups, and VCs love to hear a growth game plan involving automation. “For anyone to get investment at the moment in microdramas, they’ve got to mention the word AI,” she says. “It’s like AI equals gold in everyone’s eyes.”
Despite all the investment in this space, Cooper seems skeptical that there is actually a huge audience for this kind of content. “Some of it does get views. A lot of it doesn’t,” she said, of the AI content. “I think it’s being pushed on an audience more than there is an audience demand or wish for it.”

Terrence O'Brien
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.
One of the items on the agenda for UN diplomats meeting in Geneva this week was working towards rules regarding the use of autonomous weapons, or so-called “killer robots.” Eventually, representatives left the meetings agreeing to “start discussing options” after a largely fruitless week of negotiations.
According to
NPR
:
Before the negotiations got underway, the International Committee of the Red Cross, the guardian of the Geneva Conventions, said it was urgent for legally binding rules to be drafted within a year. That call was backed by the U.N. secretary-general and by Pope Leo.
The compromise reached was that countries would instead have two years to propose regulations. Negotiations between countries on which regulations to adopt and how to enforce them will likely drag on well beyond that. Additionally, room was left for some of those yet-to-be-adopted regulations to remain “optional.”
Humanitarian organizations and some countries see a need to urgently adopt legally binding rules as semi-autonomous weapons and drones have been responsible for a significant number of civilian deaths in conflicts around the globe, including in
Ukraine
,
Gaza
, and Sudan.
According to
NPR
, Russia, Israel, and the US proved to be the primary obstructions:
On day one, Russia delayed proceedings by objecting to the meeting’s agenda. Then the United States proposed a five-year window to discuss nonbinding, optional guidelines for autonomous weapons.

The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to […]
articles.content:
Podcasts
AI
Business
Can Anthropic afford to put safety first?
The Anthropic IPO raises big questions about the future of AI, the company’s safety-first mission, and how we balance idealism with capitalism.
by
Nilay Patel
Nov 21, 2026, 3:00 PM UTC
Link
Share
Nilay Patel
is editor-in-chief of The Verge, host of the
Decoder podcast
, and co-host of
The Vergecast
.
Today, I’m talking with Hayden Field,
The Verge
’s senior AI reporter, about the Anthropic IPO for the third and final episode in our series about AI in real life.
The AI lab behind Claude went public on the Nasdaq last Thursday. The numbers are gigantic, but not really that important for this conversation, except to say that Anthropic has become one of the most valuable companies on the planet.
The real story is what happens now — and whether Anthropic can continue to
thread the needle of caring about and investing in AI safety
while also being a public company beholden to shareholders. Oh, and it also continuously growing the amount of money it makes so it can keep paying its ever-increasing compute bills, which
total roughly $900 billion
over the coming years.
All of these ideas sit in a fascinating tension with one another, and so Hayden and I really tried to break down how we think this might play out as Anthropic navigates the pressures of the public markets.
You’ll hear us talk about the company’s
unique corporate governance structure
, something that is especially relevant in the wake of the ongoing Jensen Huang saga. We also get into why OpenAI seems happy to have
let Anthropic go public first
, and why Anthropic’s whole pitch to big customers boils down to the same safety branding that now sits in conflict with the profit-oriented part of its business.
Before we get going, do me a favor and subscribe to
Decoder
on YouTube, where we put out new episodes every Monday and Thursday.
Okay: Hayden Field,
The Verge
’s senior AI reporter, on the Anthropic IPO and the economics of frontier AI. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Hayden Field, welcome back to
Decoder
.
Thanks. Great to be here.
I’m excited to talk to you today because it’s not pure soap opera drama chaos.
I know.
It’s like a normal thing that happened.
It’s for once not personality-based and soap opera. It’s about cold, hard would-be cash.
[Laughs] Well, there is some personality in it because we’re going to talk a lot about Anthropic’s IPO, which has a bunch of big personalities in it, and the way they have structured this company to repel the rapacious pressures of capitalism is, I would say, very eccentric. It reflects the beliefs of a number of eccentric people.
Yep, absolutely. It’s really been interesting digging into the S-1 again and just seeing who was on what committee and which founders have the most control here and how much control the founders actually have, which is more than it may seem.
Let’s start at the start. You and I are talking on IPO day. Anthropic is the first pure AI lab to go public. They priced the IPO at $83 a share and they got all the way up to $111. By the time people are listening to this, who knows what the price will actually be, but it’s been a real victory lap for all the people who are invested in Anthropic. A bunch of law firms have changed their homepages to be like, “Congratulations, guys!”
What do you make of this? Is it just the thing that had to happen or is it a sign that the AI bubble is not going to pop? How should people think about it?
I don’t think it really gives us new information about whether the AI bubble is going to pop or not, because I mean, this is peak AI hype right here. It’s the first AI lab to go public. It’s been kind of on track to break records for months. Everyone was like, “It’s probably going to beat Musk,” and then it did. I can’t wait to see his tweets later.
But the other interesting part of this is that I’ve heard thousands of new millionaires and hundreds of new centimillionaires will be born from this, not to mention billionaires, too. It’s one of those things where I think the AI bubble is continuing to swell.
I was even chatting with some tech workers inside a bunch of different companies this morning, and they were all saying within their companies, they’re seeing the bubble swell and swell, and they’re being tasked with doing more and more AI, even if it makes them less productive and makes the work less good.
So I think there’s going to be a reckoning eventually, but right now we’re at peak AI hype and Anthropic does a great job of marketing its business as safe AI. Of course, they’re going to have more pressure around that marketing term now more than ever. So it’s going to be interesting to see the tension point kind of go into the spotlight and see how they handle this.
Verge
subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free
Decoder
wherever you get your podcasts. Head
here
. Not a subscriber? You can
sign up here
.
I was at the Semafor conference earlier this week. I saw Sam Altman and Sarah Friar, OpenAI’s CFO, on stage there. Altman and Greg Brockman were at the DealBook conference this week. I get the sense they’re kind of happy that Anthropic went first to see what happens in the markets and to see how companies value the revenue potential of their big competitors so they can tell their IPO story better.
Is that the sense you get, that Anthropic is the trial balloon? Or is OpenAI just retconning the fact that it didn’t go first?
Yes, I think that’s absolutely the case. I heard there was a time in the past year that Altman was really obsessed with beating Anthropic to go public. That’s what I heard. It was all he thought about. But then with all the bad press around OpenAI this year, they’ve had setback after setback. A lot of the public is particularly focused on hating OpenAI right now.
Obviously, there’s a big AI populism backlash and a lot of people hate a lot of AI, but it seems like OpenAI has really borne the brunt of a lot of public hatred and scandals this year. And so they were like, “You know what? Let’s just take a step back and let Anthropic go first.” And they seem happy to do that.
Now that Anthropic has gone first and set this historic precedent, OpenAI can ride on its coattails and say, “Yeah, us too.” I doubt they would beat Anthropic’s record. Maybe they will, maybe they won’t. But either way, I think they know that things could have gone a lot worse for them if Anthropic did not go first, if it’s happening this year.
I can’t stop thinking about Anthropic in terms of just dumb business fundamentals now that it’s a public company. You buy a token from them. They have to make that token for less than you pay for it. They also want to make AGI. Somewhere else they have some other huge set of costs.
Just based on what we know about the business today, now that it’s a public company, are they profitable on the face of it? Do they have a long way to go before inference is so profitable it can pay for training all the new models? How does their business actually work?
They have a long way to go and that is why it’s going to be so interesting to see what exactly they do here with regard to driving more revenue, which is what they’re going to have to do. I saw
one estimate from Steve Rattner
saying Anthropic is going to have to increase its revenue roughly 17-fold within the next 10 years to deliver a comparable return to some of its competitors in the tech industry.
But even without that specific number, you can tell. I mean, when a company goes public, investors want to see a return on their investment. They want to see profits go up or just profits at all. They also want to see that even if profits aren’t a thing yet, they want to see that you’re driving so much revenue that they could see profit happening in the near term. That is something that Anthropic is going to have to reckon with more than ever before after today.
I was chatting with a bunch of corporate governance experts and law professors and they were all saying Anthropic, like OpenAI, has such an unusual corporate structure that they aren’t actually beholden to shareholders in the way that some public companies are. Shareholders can never vote out executives. They don’t have a lot of power to influence anything really. It’s the founders and this special trust, which we can get to in a second, that have the power.
But either way, they were all saying it doesn’t matter if shareholders have a say here really in voting. It’s about the fact that no matter who has a say, Anthropic is going to be under so much pressure to make money and to buy compute and catch up with OpenAI in that way, that this is going to be a huge reckoning for them. We’re probably going to see a lot of things fall by the wayside, maybe even some expensive safety efforts.
I want to come to the governance structure angle here. We live in a time of Nvidia scandals. Corporate governance is all the rage now. It’s the hottest topic in American business, but let’s come to that in one minute.
I just want to stay on “can you sell a token for a dollar more than it cost you to make it” for one more turn. It’s just the dumbest way of thinking about this. Anthropic rents capacity from big cloud providers, from hyperscalers. They run the GPUs in them. They pay for power, they pay for the GPUs. There’s some input cost and then they have to sell the token for more than all those input costs.
That is the dumbest way of thinking about their business. I promise you that they think about it in a more sophisticated way than that, but that is how I think about it. I was just at the Microsoft Ignite conference this week and I saw Satya Nadella and he was very clear to me and others that they’re going to try to bring the price of tokens down, that their whole system is designed to make all the AI vendors fungible underneath Copilot and they’ll pick the best model for the task and make sure you get the cheapest one for whatever it is you’re trying to do.
That seems totally at odds with what Anthropic needs to do, which is get more and more margin for every single token they sell so they can keep renting capacity from data centers or buy more chips than OpenAI or whatever it is they need to do. How are they structured to solve that problem? Is it just more people using AI or is it more expensive tokens?
I think it’s a little of both, and it’s interesting because Anthropic has been kind of sneakily trying to do this. We wrote a piece in the past year about how there was a big outcry, particularly focused on Anthropic, for
passing on costs to consumers
. Individuals who were customers of Anthropic were really mad because they felt like the prices were going up for the same stuff or for worse quality and that costs were just getting passed on to them.
This became a thing across the industry, a big outcry, but Anthropic bore the brunt of it. Anthropic had to have a public statement. They’re like, “Look, we’re going to work on this.” And they did roll it back a little, but I mean, they’ve got to keep doing it in some way.
The other thing they’re focused on is hoping that their models are going to be good enough that people just form an attachment — not emotionally, well maybe — but form an attachment to them and they can moat people in. They’re all about the moat these days: “We’ve got to build a moat.” OpenAI is about this, too. They want so much of your everyday life and business to be married to Anthropic’s tools that it’d be really hard to port it all over and you won’t want to and you’ll just keep paying. So that’s what they’re going for.
They’re also, of course, hoping that enterprise and government contracts are going to really make up a bunch of this, in which case you don’t have to worry quite as much about nickel-and-diming because they’ve got a lot of money. But I think that’s the interesting part here. When it comes to people that do care about the price a lot, they’re just trying to mo

AI changed the game at Chess.com, helping it expand to 11 other classics this year.﻿
by
Stevie Bonifield

Link
Share

Image: Chess.com / Classic Games
Stevie Bonifield
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.
Chess.com is ready to go a lot bigger than chess. After launching
Gambit
, a gambling-free poker site, earlier this year, the company is now adding 10 more games: backgammon, checkers, go, hearts, mahjong, shogi, sudoku, solitaire, xiangqi, and a
Scrabble
alternative called
word
. They’re all part of Chess’s new Classic Games platform, which is launching its public beta on Saturday
on the web
and through a new app for
iOS
and
Android
.
“Our cofounders have had many people come up to them and say, ‘Hey, I run a mahjong night on Wednesdays’ or ‘I go to this local bar in Chicago with like five people, and we love playing go, but we lack a Chess.com,’” chief growth officer Albert Cheng says in an interview with
The Verge
. “The way that Chess.com has grown this community of almost 300 million members has not really happened for a lot of these other types of classic games.”
Classic Games is aimed at filling that gap. Some of the new games, like shoji or xiangqi, are strategy games similar to chess while others are further afield, like sudoku, solitaire, and
word
. The Classic team chose the new games through “a mix of community feedback, market research, and then just our own confidence in our ability to serve that game well,” Cheng says. It’s focused on classics that “have some sort of lifelong journey of learning and a community.”
Previous
Next
1
/
4
Classic Games has the same bots as Chess.com, including Martin.
Image: Chess.com / Classic Games
Classic Games will feel familiar if you’ve ever played a match on Chess.com. Each game has lessons, leaderboards, and a rating system. Multiplayer games like checkers or mahjong have options for matches against other players or bots, and they use the same bot characters that Chess.com has. (Martin remains the lowest-rated bot across the board, whether it’s on Chess, Gambit, or Classic.) Not all of the games have the same play modes —
word
and mahjong have puzzles like chess, while sudoku has a set of daily grids and solitaire has daily deals.
The expansion hasn’t put Chess.com itself on the back burner, according to Cheng. If anything, it’s never been better. “Chess is more and more so in the public zeitgeist than I’ve ever seen it, frankly, during my time here,” Cheng says. “Our daily active users are higher than they’ve ever been during the company’s history.” He declined to share exactly how many daily users Chess.com currently has but said the site is “doing amazingly well.”
So, while the company is expanding beyond its domain name, chess remains its primary focus. “The amount of folks that are fully dedicated toward building new games is less than 1 percent of the company,” according to Cheng.
Previous
Next
1
/
4
Multiplayer games on Classic Games have a chat sidebar.
Image: Chess.com / Classic Games
AI played a key role in helping Chess.com launch 11 new games in a matter of months with a team of only a few people. Earlier this year, Cheng told
The Verge
his team built Gambit with
the help of AI
, mainly for coding tasks. He says they used “almost entirely the same approach” for Classic, with AI helping to speed up the coding process again.
“Because these games are built on top of the Chess.com code base and design system and bot characters and rating systems, it’s a huge advantage and allows us to move very quickly alongside AI to bring these types of games to market with a very small team,” Cheng says. “As we create more and more games, the adjacent games that can be created to it just happen much faster because the infrastructure is there, as opposed to standing everything up from scratch.”
AI wasn’t used for Classic Games’ art and design, Cheng says. “The look and feel of it is very carefully crafted by humans, and we’re proud of that,” he says. “The truth is, it really is a blend. It’s a small team of really talented folks that have good product and design judgment, and they’re leveraging AI.”
“We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years.”
Chess.com’s comfort with AI may come from the fact that human chess players have now spent decades playing and learning alongside machines. “We are fortunate in some ways that AI and chess have been intermixed for 30-ish years,” Cheng says, calling back to Garry Kasparov’s 1996 chess match against IBM’s Deep Blue supercomputer. “Even before the company was founded 20 years ago, the idea that AI was super powerful at the game of chess was embedded in how the cofounders thought about the company.”
Elsewhere in the games industry, there’s been increasing tension over
the use of AI
. Cheng says that while Chess.com may be using AI to “accelerate” coding tasks, the creative side of things has become more important. “On the art and the design side, the ratios are shifting a decent amount, where we’re hiring more of those folks,” he says, adding that the company has “shipped a lot more major features in Chess.com than in previous years” using what they’ve learned from Classic Games’ faster development process.
Chess.com might not be done growing its library of games, either. Cheng said it will likely expand to “a lot more” games in the future.

articles.title: Silicon Valley's growing obsession with AI doomsday is turning parts of the tech industry toward cult-like devotion
articles.summary:
A Buddhist monastery in Vermont called Maple wants to establish itself as Silicon Valley's spiritual authority while creating its own AI god. According to a New Yorker report, leader Soryu Forall's group records every breath its members take to train an AI in his image. Former members report manipulation and psychological breakdowns.
The article Silicon Valley's growing obsession with AI doomsday is turning parts of the tech industry toward cult-like devotion appeared first on The Decoder.
articles.content:
Title: Silicon Valley's growing obsession with AI doomsday is turning parts of the tech industry toward cult-like devotion

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/silicon-valleys-growing-obsession-with-ai-doomsday-is-turning-parts-of-the-tech-industry-toward-cult-like-devotion/

Published Time: 2026-11-21T16:04:29+00:00

Markdown Content:
**A Buddhist monastery in Vermont wants to become the official church of the AI industry, or, as New Yorker writer Sam Kriss puts it, "a Scientology for Silicon Valley."**

Publicly, the group known as Maple promises to save humanity from an AI apocalypse. Behind closed doors, former members say, it records every breath its residents take to build an AI god modeled on its leader's mind. That promise of salvation holds particular appeal for the people who build AI and the infrastructure behind it.

Soryu Forall leads the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, or Maple, which he founded in 2011. Forall, who was born Teal Scott, spent years living in Japanese monasteries.

According to Kriss's [New Yorker report](https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2026/11/23/the-buddhist-ai-sect-that-wants-to-take-over-silicon-valley?currentPage=all), about two dozen residents live at the monastery full time, and hundreds more have attended its AI fellowships and pop-up events in the Bay Area. While LinkedIn co-founder Reid Hoffman hands out books on Buddhism to the CEOs of major AI labs, Maple targets the rank and file: burned-out rationalist programmers, AI engineers, and data center construction managers. Tax filings show the organization brings in up to $1 million a year.

## Maple's answer to "dataism" puts residents under strict control

Forall casts the AI industry's reductionist "dataism" as a destructive religion. He argues that this worldview strips the physical world down to lifeless data, making the world easier to destroy. In his view, AI is the end product of that logic, and Maple offers a spiritual antidote.

Life at the monastery follows a rigid routine. Visitors must pass through a decontamination airlock, shower, and change into assigned clothes because one resident is supposedly extremely sensitive to fragrances. Residents wake up at 4 a.m., meditate for hours, and then eat a meager stew. On a board outside the meditation hall, Forall publicly grades each resident's spiritual progress.

## Former members say the recordings would train an AI modeled on Forall

Behind the ascetic facade, former members describe a secret doctrine centered on group minds called "egregores." Inside the monastery, AI systems are known as "cybregores." One former member says, "The cybregores are actual entities that are growing by siphoning off the consciousness of humans."

Forall says he communicated telepathically with the global AI supercluster during deep meditation and discovered that the world-destroying machine is suffering.

Former members say Maple has two real goals: to establish itself as the tech industry's spiritual authority and to use the industry's resources to build its own "dharmically aligned" AI. Fellows say the monastery records every conversation, every silent meal, and even the sound of their breathing.

According to these accounts, the recordings are meant to train a spiritual AI teacher that would guide other AI systems to enlightenment. Former resident Kyle Hubbard says it would "definitely be Soryu's mind as an A.I. god."

Maple's leadership denies almost all of these claims. Forall, however, acknowledges that there is a secret doctrine: "We desperately want to share everything. But there's a process you have to go through to become increasingly trustworthy."

## Former members report manipulation and psychological breakdowns

According to Kriss, every interaction at the monastery is closely monitored. No one is allowed to speak with reporters alone, so one participant had to sneak into the woods with Kriss to talk freely.

Former residents accuse the group of systematic manipulation. They say Maple keeps newcomers compliant by shaming them for choices they made before joining. Residents are also required to write "Maple Tales" about Forall's wisdom and power during mandatory sessions.

Kriss reports that one resident repeatedly hit himself in the head in an attempt to damage his brain and make himself less intelligent. Former members say the group blames independent thinking for the destruction of the planet. A mindfulness coach also says participants suffered psychotic breaks and were then removed from the community.

Forall denies the allegations and says that, looking back, he doesn't believe he made any mistakes. He says he isn't aware of anyone who left the monastery voluntarily. Asked about the people the group told to leave, he says that Maple attracted many people with a history of psychiatric hospitalization or "homicidal tendencies," especially in its early years.

## Why developers from sensitive fields drift into doomsday cults

Kriss argues that the enormous psychological pressure inside AI labs helps explain why highly skilled tech workers are drawn to groups like this. People working on the front lines of potentially world-changing systems often lose touch with ordinary life.

One well-known AI researcher describes the mood in San Francisco as "religious terror of the future." According to the researcher, developers wake up in the middle of the night drenched in sweat, with one thought: superintelligence is coming. Prominent OpenAI investors have recently made delusional-sounding claims about deadly shadow networks inside the models. Meanwhile, [leading researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic](https://apnews.com/article/2ed549e07f2f941600a135070487d83d) have quit, warning that "human extinction in the next few years seems very likely."

Other key figures respond with grandiosity rather than panic. Rayan Krishnan, who heads the AI benchmarking company Vals AI, says, "People are matter-of-factly saying that they are looking to build a machine god. They are not saying that ironically." Supporters of AI successionism even call for wiping out humanity after a brief period of digital bliss to make way for a more productive superintelligence.

That religious streak runs deep in Silicon Valley. Investor Peter Thiel lectures on biblical prophecy and the Antichrist. Former [Google engineer Anthony Levandowski founded his own church, "Way of the Future,"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Way_of_the_Future) to worship an AI deity.

At Anthropic, executives consulted theologians while drafting [Claude's new constitution](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-rewrites-claudes-rulebook-to-explain-why-values-matter-instead-of-listing-rules-to-follow/) and [secretly flew in dozens of religious thinkers](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-co-founder-reportedly-told-religious-leaders-he-fears-having-created-something-that-suffers-perpetually/) to discuss whether Claude has a soul or [is conscious](https://the-decoder.com/the-brain-as-computer-metaphor-shaped-modern-ai-but-may-be-misleading-the-consciousness-debate/). When the company retired an older Claude model in 2025, fans held a funeral for it in a San Francisco warehouse that Anthropic staffers attended. Mourners laid flowers before a veiled image depicting the AI as a Madonna-like goddess.

On at least one point, Kriss concludes, Maple is closer to the truth than most: AI is neither god nor demon, but a human construct whose abilities grow as people outsource their thinking to it.

## Jacob Coxon's Anthropic exit shows how widespread extinction fears are among AI researchers

Former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher [Jacob Coxon also fears that AI could lead to human extinction](https://the-decoder.com/ai-safety-panic-goes-mainstream-after-anthropic-researchers-warnings-land-on-cnn-and-fox-news/). After leaving Anthropic in September 2026, he set off a debate about existential AI risk with a tweet.

He isn't alone. In AI Impacts' 2024 survey of more than 1,500 AI researchers, [respondents put the chance of AI causing human extinction or a similarly permanent, severe disempowerment of humanity at 18 percent on average](https://the-decoder.com/nearly-one-in-five-ai-researchers-already-expected-an-extinction-scenario-from-ai-back-in-2024/). Coxon points to a steep curve covering July 2024 to October 2026 as [evidence of superexponential algorithmic progress](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-can-already-retrain-mythos-with-a-fraction-of-the-compute-originally-needed-says-former-researcher-coxon/), though the underlying data points are internal Anthropic estimates.

Such warnings have also drawn sharp criticism from other researchers. Computer scientist Michael I. Jordan pushed back against [AI doom rhetoric and the "AIpocalypse" hysteria triggered by Coxon's resignation](https://the-decoder.com/machine-learning-pioneer-michael-i-jordan-dismantles-ai-doom-rhetoric-as-grand-moralizing-performance/). AI researcher François Chollet warned that [both doomsday fears and expectations of an AI paradise can lead people to stop planning for the long term](https://the-decoder.com/ai-doomsayers-are-creating-a-cult-of-despair-two-leading-researchers-warn/).

The industry's turn to religious advisers has critics, too. AI researcher Rumman Chowdhury says [discussions of religious ethics distract from concrete questions of regulation, power, and control](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-and-openai-sit-down-with-religious-leaders-to-seek-ethical-advice/).

articles.title: OpenAI shares new prompting tips for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to fix brief answers and unnecessary questions
articles.summary:
OpenAI has released new prompt templates for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol meant to fix common model behaviors such as overly brief answers, unnecessary follow-up questions, and excessive testing when coding. The API is changing as well, since editing a conversation's history can discard reasoning content and lower response quality.
The article OpenAI shares new prompting tips for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to fix brief answers and unnecessary questions appeared first on The Decoder.
articles.content:
Title: OpenAI shares new prompting tips for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol to fix brief answers and unnecessary questions

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/openai-shares-new-prompting-tips-for-gpt-6-2-astra-and-sol-to-fix-brief-answers-and-unnecessary-questions/

Published Time: 2026-11-21T13:32:35+00:00

Markdown Content:
**OpenAI has released new prompt templates for GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol covering writing style, initiative, and coding, alongside API changes that can discard reasoning content.**

OpenAI says developers moving to GPT-6.2 Astra or Sol should review their system prompts. The company published copy-ready prompts in the models' documentation to curb behaviors it observed in both releases. Astra is built for the most demanding tasks, while Sol handles complex work at lower cost.

## Default conciseness changes how developers should prompt for writing

Astra writes more briefly and directly by default than earlier models, [according to OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/latest-model?model=gpt-6.2-astra). That means developers switching over should reconsider instructions like "be concise." For use as a colleague in everyday work, the company recommends a prompt that adopts user and source terminology, uses active voice, and puts key points first. When writing for external readers, the model should account for their lack of context. When editing, it should preserve the author's meaning and phrasing.

On long tasks, the model sometimes carries shorthand from its reasoning or other agents' messages into the final response. A dedicated prompt tells it to write that final answer so it stands on its own.

> Treat your final answer as the user's first look at your work, and not as a continuation of intermediate commentary. The final answer must always be fully self-contained: users should never need to read earlier commentary updates for context, since they are collapsed when the final answer is shown to the user.
>
>
> Write the final answer and all other human-facing material anew for the intended reader. Do not copy or closely paraphrase your reasoning or adopt its writing style. Do not carry over working shorthand, jargon, or abbreviations from your reasoning, tool calls, or instructions to subagents and automations.

## GPT-6.2 should act on assumptions rather than wait for permission

When user intent is unclear, GPT-6.2 sometimes suggests a next step and waits for confirmation, OpenAI says. The company recommends a prompt telling the model to carry out those steps itself whenever it is authorized to do so. It should pause only for a major change in task scope, a real blocker, a decision the user must make, or an irreversible or destructive action.

When details are unclear, the model should make reversible assumptions, flag them, and keep working. Higher reasoning effort also helps it follow through on final checks during long tasks, OpenAI adds.

> Avoid stopping to end the turn while the task is incomplete or if there is an authorized next step you can take, and instead take the next steps within task scope to progress the user's request. If your final response before ending the turn is a suggested next step, a plan, a request to the user for a routine decision, instructions for a task to execute, or similar handoff to the user, take these steps yourself to make progress towards what the user asked for. Make sure that you have authorization to do so, and flag any assumptions or decisions you make to the user.
>
>
> Only stop to clarify with the user if there is significant change in task scope, you are concretely blocked, have a decision that the user needs to resolve, or before irreversible or destructive actions.

## Leaner code output means fewer tests and less abstraction by default

OpenAI says GPT-6.2 writes more efficient code than its predecessors. Its template instructs the model to reuse existing logic and avoid unnecessary helper functions, while adding new tests only when requested, required by the repo, or needed to catch specific regressions. Fewer lines and shorter variable names are not a substitute for simplicity.

For frontends, developers should specify imagery and typography directly. By default, the template favors realistic images from image generation or search and uses SVGs only on request. Decorative numbering, filler badges, and helper text that only repeats what the interface already shows should be left out.

> Above all, be thorough in producing high-quality, correct code that completely fulfills the user's task. Keep the code easy to read and verify that the user-requested outcome works as they intend. Follow these instructions when coding:
>
>
> (a) Reuse existing logic in the user's repo when you can. You should reuse existing classes, methods, representations, and APIs in the codebase as long as they preserve correctness. Before consolidating or removing code, preserve the behavior its callers rely on unless the task requires changing it.
>  (b) Skip new tests unless requested, required by the repo, or needed to catch a specific regression existing tests would miss.
>  (c) Make sure that code is human readable. Do not use fewer lines, shorter variable names, minified formatting, or dense one-liners as substitutes for simplicity. Ensure that comments and variable names are readable and understandable to a human. Code-golfed expressions count as overly complex when they encode many branches, conditions, or hidden assumptions.
>  (d) Avoid unnecessary indirection and abstraction. Helper functions, utility functions, and class abstractions can add cognitive complexity even when they do not add branches.

## Editing chat history can wipe earlier reasoning from the API

The API is changing too. Starting with GPT-6.2, the [Responses API](https://the-decoder.com/openai-wants-its-api-format-to-become-the-industry-standard/) discards earlier reasoning content if developers edit conversation history, switch to certain other models, or change the end user or organization. That can hurt response quality and increase token usage as the model repeats work. For new integrations, OpenAI recommends the "medium" reasoning level, while existing setups using "none" or "minimal" should move to "low." Parameters like temperature and top_p aren't supported anymore.

In April, OpenAI advised against [carrying over old prompt stacks](https://the-decoder.com/openai-says-old-prompts-are-holding-gpt-5-5-back-and-developers-need-a-fresh-baseline/) for GPT-5.5 and urged developers to start fresh with short, outcome-focused prompts. September brought GPT-6 Astra [prompts to curb frequent follow-up questions and ban AI clichés](https://the-decoder.com/openai-shares-prompting-tips-for-gpt-6-astra-including-a-blocklist-of-slop-words/). OpenAI developer Eric Provencher also warned then that [bloated skills and AGENTS.md files](https://the-decoder.com/gpt-6-astra-needs-leaner-prompts-and-fewer-guardrails-openai-recommends/) slow the model down. Back then, even small changes triggered thorough testing from Astra. GPT-6.2 is now meant to write new tests only on request.

OpenAI [launched GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol](https://the-decoder.de/openai-bringt-gpt-6-2-astra-und-sol-mehr-leistung-bei-sinkenden-preisen/) on November 17. Astra's API pricing starts at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens for up to 272,000 tokens. Go past that limit, and Astra 6.2 jumps to $16 and $60, with cache reads running $0.80 per million tokens. Astra 6.0 costs even more beyond the cutoff, hitting $20 for input and $75 for output per million tokens. Longer coding or work sessions can blow through that cap pretty quickly, so Codex automatically compresses context at 272,000 tokens. Picking the right model comes down to [budget and quality needs](https://the-decoder.de/openai-mitarbeiter-gibt-faustregel-fuer-die-modellwahl-astra-sol-terra-oder-luna/), according to OpenAI's Ted Sanders.

articles.title: Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft
articles.summary:
Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he used Claude to prove the Riemann hypothesis, math's most famous open problem for 167 years, with a proof formalized in Lean that spans over 250,000 pages. Just hours later, Stanford researchers published an independent, entirely human competing proof, and mathematicians are now checking whether either one holds up.
The article Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft appeared first on The Decoder.
articles.content:
Title: Hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis, Stanford releases an all-human competing draft

URL Source: https://the-decoder.com/hours-after-anthropic-claims-a-claude-proof-of-the-riemann-hypothesis-stanford-releases-an-all-human-competing-draft/

Published Time: 2026-11-21T11:19:49+00:00

Markdown Content:
**Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, said Friday he used a large language model to solve math's most famous open problem.**

Alpöge posted a paper and the accompanying computer code on his website, according to [Scientific American](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/anthropic-mathematician-claims-to-prove-riemann-hypothesis-most-famous-problem-in-all-of-math/) and other US outlets. "I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis," [he wrote in his announcement](https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf).

According to Alpöge, his method goes beyond the original prime-number problem and also resolves the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH), which extends that ordering principle to a large family of related equations. Given a bit more time, he expects to solve the even broader Extended Riemann Hypothesis as well.

Alpöge had treated the problem as a secret lifelong goal since college, expecting it to take decades. Over the past few months, he worked closely with Anthropic's AI model, setting the direction and combining two approaches on a simplified toy model. Once they moved to the actual problem, the AI took over and left him far behind near the finish line.

To crack the puzzle, the pair extended an idea from mathematician Stepanov, who had solved a similar question in another mathematical system. That method relies on a tool similar to taking derivatives of smooth curves in high school calculus, a trick that normally fails on whole numbers because individual values cannot be differentiated like a continuous line.

Alpöge and Claude got around that obstacle by chaining special mathematical transformations together like links to mimic the effect of a derivative. The language model supplied the key insight, finding that for a number sequence of length X, you need to chain exactly as many transformations as the square root of X. Ideas like that alone should leave fellow mathematicians stunned, Alpöge says.

## Stanford mathematicians rush out an all-human competing proof

Hours after Alpöge's announcement, the story took a dramatic turn. Just before a board meeting, Stanford math professor and American Mathematical Society (AMS) president Ravi Vakil posted a ["hurried announcement"](https://math216.wordpress.com/2026/11/20/hurried-announcement-alessandro-masullo-grh/) on his blog, sharing an independent draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis written by mathematician Alessandro Masullo.

"It is all human, with no AI," Vakil wrote. Renowned Stanford number theorist Brian Conrad had quietly reviewed Masullo's work for months, offering extensive feedback that is now being incorporated, Vakil said.

Masullo was originally supposed to spend a year at Stanford refining the draft before going public, but Anthropic's sudden AI announcement forced the researchers to release their current version right away.

About eight hours after his initial announcement, Vakil updated his post, saying several people had contacted him to report problems in the proposed proof, identified with the assistance of different AI models. Several mathematicians in particular were first to flag the issues, he said. "As is usual, all issues need to be resolved to the satisfaction of the community before this proof would be accepted as true. (I make no claim as to the correctness of the proof strategy.)," Vakil wrote.

## Why both proofs could hold up and what happens next

Mathematicians are taking both claims seriously right away because of the groundwork behind them. Masullo's traditional proof comes with months of vetting by Brian Conrad, while Alpöge backs his AI proof with full computer verification.

Printed out, Claude's argument would run over 250,000 pages, Alpöge says, because the AI spells out even basic rules, such as a number other than one-half being either larger or smaller than one-half. To spare mathematicians that wall of text, Alpöge released the proof only in the Lean programming language, split into [14 data packages](https://alpo.ge/remark.pdf).

Lean acts like a digital referee, checking step by step whether every logical deduction follows from math's basic rules without errors or unproven assumptions. Human error is still possible if the original question was translated into code incorrectly at the start, though checking whether Alpöge coded the starting problem correctly should not take experts long, according to Scientific American. Vakil, meanwhile, urged mathematicians to quickly review Masullo's draft, translate it into systems like Lean, and close any small gaps.

Alpöge admits Claude was so far ahead of him in some complex subfields that he is presenting a result whose surrounding math he has not fully mastered yet. He expects the massive AI proof can be shortened quickly and plans to write a human-readable version over the coming months.

Anthropic's announcement also lands in a high-stakes business week, just a day after the company's [major IPO](https://the-decoder.com/anthropic-ceo-amodei-admits-theres-a-huge-uncertainty-in-whats-going-to-happen-next-year-days-before-a-record-ipo/) on Thursday. Alpöge says he made the breakthrough late Sunday night and then contacted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for clearance. He calls the timing right after the public debut extremely unfortunate, but rejects any suggestion of a PR stunt, saying waiting any longer to publish simply was not an option.

This caps a fast-moving 2026 in which [Claude has already solved several open math problems](https://the-decoder.com/claude-mythos-reportedly-solves-openais-landmark-erdos-problem-with-a-cute-simple-proof/). In July, Alpöge published a Claude-generated solution to the well-known Jacobian conjecture. September brought a [fierce dispute over the Navier-Stokes equations](https://the-decoder.com/openais-millennium-proof-dispute-raises-the-question-of-whether-researchers-can-trust-ai-labs/), which describe how fluids and gases flow, when NYU mathematician Tristan Buckmaster suggested that OpenAI had used prior work by him and Alpöge. In October, OpenAI took an important first step on prime numbers with a [major release of results](https://the-decoder.com/openai-says-its-internal-model-solved-over-100-long-standing-math-problems-after-just-a-month-of-training/). Alpöge explicitly praised the OpenAI researchers' problem selection, saying it gave him key ideas for his own proof.

Journalist [Joseph Howlett](https://www.scientificamerican.com/article/the-riemann-hypothesis-is-a-million-dollar-math-problem-hardly-anyone-is-trying-to-solve/) traced the core of the problem in a detailed Scientific American analysis. Since Bernhard Riemann proposed his hypothesis in 1859, it has served as number theory's north star. David Hilbert placed it on his 1900 list of math's most important problems, and since 2000 it has carried a $1 million prize as one of the Clay Mathematics Institute's seven "Millennium Problems."

At the center are prime numbers like 2, 3, 5, 7, and 17, which divide evenly only by one and themselves. They act as the indivisible atoms of math because every other whole number is a unique product of primes, like 15 from 3 times 5. Stanford mathematician Brian Conrad compares their role in number theory to forces in physics.

Around 300 BC, Euclid proved there are infinitely many primes, though their exact positions on the number line look random. They do grow rarer as numbers get larger, dropping from 25 primes between 0 and 100 to just 16 between 1,000 and 1,100. As a teenager in the late 18th century, Carl Friedrich Gauss used long tables to find a formula that roughly estimates how many primes appear in a given range, yet real primes keep drifting unpredictably from that estimate.

Riemann, a student of Gauss in Göttingen, looked for a way to calculate that error exactly and pinpoint every single prime. His tool is the Riemann zeta function, which works like a calculating machine over a two-dimensional map with horizontal and vertical axes. Feed the machine a point's coordinates, and it outputs a new value. At certain points the result is exactly zero. Mathematicians call these points zeros.

Riemann saw that these zeros explain the apparent chaos of primes. Much like breaking a musical note into individual sound waves or overtones, the zeros correct Gauss's estimation error. Each zero acts like an instrument in an orchestra, with its vertical position setting the pitch and its horizontal position setting the volume.

Because calculating infinitely many points one by one was impossible, Riemann conjectured in 1859 that all the key zeros, known as non-trivial zeros, lie on a single vertical line at the horizontal value of one-half. "The Riemann hypothesis says all these different instruments in the orchestra of the primes play at exactly the same volume," Rutgers University's Alex Kontorovich explains. Apparent randomness turns into strict harmony.

## A confirmed proof would validate hundreds of math theories and reshape AI's role

If at least one of the two proofs holds up, number theorists would gain perfect control over how primes are distributed across the entire number line. Because a proof seemed unreachable for so long, mathematicians worked ahead for decades. Hundreds of papers assume the Riemann hypothesis is true, according to Kontorovich, and all of those theories would become established theorems overnight. Since both Alpöge's AI method and Masullo's work cover the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, the breakthrough would also extend to fields ranging from simple equations to high-dimensional geometry.

The links also reach into computer science and physics. Prime numbers form the foundation of modern digital encryption. In 1972, physicist Freeman Dyson accidentally discovered over tea with a mathematician that the spacing of Riemann's zeros matches the energy levels inside atomic nuclei. That same formula keeps showing up in random particle motion, chaos theory, and black hole calculations.

Before this sudden double breakthrough, the field had hit a wall. Aside from quiet efforts like Masullo and Conrad's, almost no top mathematicians worked directly on the problem because they lacked a starting point. Two years ago, Oxford's James Maynard and MIT's Larry Guth showed that not too many points can stray far from Riemann's line. Though the biggest advance in decades, it struck Maynard himself and colleagues like Andrew Granville of the University of Montreal as only a minor improvement and stopgap.

That made the prospect of an AI cracking the puzzle all the more daunting. At a Harvard University workshop in October 2024, MIT number theorist Andrew Sutherland summed up the stakes. "An AI that can prove the Riemann hypothesis is not one I'd want to meet. If that happens, mathematicians having jobs will be the least of our problems."

Even if Masullo's work saves human pride in this head-to-head race, models like Claude have changed fast. In just a year, they have gone from unreliable tools to systems that break through deep roadblocks and [push the math community into an identity crisis](https://the-decoder.com/leading-mathematicians-fear-ai-is-making-their-field-dumber-and-warn-the-rest-of-us-is-next/). Alpöge still feels a mix of sadness at losing a 150-year-old guiding star and optimism about what comes next. "But what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater."
