# New open model Inkling 2 Mini thinks in loops to solve problems with fewer words and still runs on a laptop

**Thinking Machines has released Inkling 2 Mini, a so-called looped transformer.** A looped transformer runs certain layers multiple times for each token. Inkling 2 Mini runs 12 of its 24 layers three times in a row. That lets the model reason internally for longer without generating more text, finding the right answer with fewer tokens, [according to Thinking Machines](https://thinkingmachines.ai/news/inkling-2-mini/#capabilities). The open mixture-of-experts model has 26.4 billion parameters, with 5.4 billion active per token because of the loops, the company says. It processes text and images, has a 1-million-token context window, and is licensed under Apache 2.0.

Inkling 2 Mini leads all open models under 100 billion parameters on agentic coding tests, scoring 48.2 percent on DeepSWE v1.1 and 46.5 percent on the Vals Index v2.2. [Artificial Analysis](https://artificialanalysis.ai/articles/inkling-2-mini) gives it 20 points on its Intelligence Index, tying it with Qwen3.8 27B at roughly six times lower cost and four times the speed.

Inkling 2 Mini scores 20 on Artificial Analysis's Intelligence Index, tying it with Qwen3.8 27B (xhigh) and Nanbeige4.3-33B. With far fewer active parameters, the model sits directly on the Pareto frontier. | Image: Artificial Analysis

Inkling 2 Mini runs locally on Macs with at least 32 GB of memory and on Nvidia's DGX Spark. You can [download the weights and a research version with variable loops from Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini). It is also available to try in the [Tinker Playground](https://tinker.thinkingmachines.ai/playground?utm_source=blog&utm_campaign=inkling_2_mini_model_release).

That leaves the index 20 percent below its October peak and in bear market territory, [according to the Financial Times](https://www.ft.com/content/9f3c6ed6-c08f-4710-9683-ee2f5eb25841). Meanwhile, high oil costs from the [Iran war](https://the-decoder.com/u-s-military-strikes-3000-targets-in-iran-with-ai-support-but-oversight-remains-underinvested/) are fueling persistent inflation and keeping interest rates high.

Nvidia took the hardest hit on Friday, plunging 14 percent after reports that the [SEC](https://the-decoder.com/sec-probes-nvidia-over-undisclosed-chip-sales-tied-to-china/) is reviewing its accounting. The US semiconductor index also dropped 10.7 percent, with losses across memory and chip stocks including Sandisk, Micron, and Broadcom. Researchers from Columbia University and CertiK have introduced
TensorLean
, a framework for formal verification of GPU kernels at the PTX level. TensorLean is a Lean-based verifier that proves compiled kernels match a tensor-level math spec. The research team
checked 149 kernel instances
, including every kernel of FlashAttention-2, -3 and -4 plus DeepGEMM. It proved 83 correct. The remaining 66 led to 38 correctness bugs.
TL;DR
Size:
1.8K-line PTX parser. Specs total 10,278 lines against 151,285 lines of kernel source, a ratio near 15:1.
Runs on:
A 16-core workstation. It checks PTX compiled for A100, H100 and B200 kernels.
Performance:
83 of 149 kernel instances proved correct, 38 bugs found across 6 projects.
Best:
Caught a FlashAttention-4 data race that never appeared in 17,760 test runs.
What is TensorLean?
TensorLean is a
formal verification framework
for GPU kernels at the PTX level.
It starts from unmodified source code. A developer writes a tensor-level spec in Lean. TensorLean then proves 4 properties: no data races, termination, correct output within tolerance, and untouched memory elsewhere.
How does TensorLean verify a GPU kernel?
Specs build on Lean’s Mathlib. Tensor operators follow PyTorch names, so
@
means
torch.matmul
. Each spec has 5 parts:
spec_math
,
spec_mut
,
spec_layout
,
spec_tol
and
requires
. The math stays separate from the memory layout.
The
pipeline
runs in 7 steps:
Start from unmodified source.
Write the tensor-level spec.
Compile to PTX and load a PTX semantics.
Build a happens-before graph to check races and termination.
Symbolically execute to get final memory, identical across schedules.
Lower the spec to PTX-memory level.
Discharge proofs with Lean’s kernel, Z3 and cvc5.
Which techniques make it scale?
Concurrency to sequential:
Race-freedom proofs on the happens-before graph cover all CTAs, threads and loop iterations symbolically.
Loop invariants over semirings:
Closed forms for tiled, accumulating loops, such as online softmax, need 1 SMT query per loop.
Tolerance proofs:
Algebraic error is proved zero. Round-off error is bounded separately, then combined.
Assertions as hints:
Developers add
tensorlean_assert
in source. Each is proved once, then reused.
What bugs did TensorLean find?
The
GitHub README
lists 38 bugs, all reported upstream. FlashAttention accounts for 23. Liger Kernel has 7, TileOPs 3, TileLang 2, DeepGEMM 2 and Triton 1.
By category,
the site reports
19 memory access errors and 13 numerical bugs. It also counts 7 data races, 5 uninitialized memory reads and 5 undefined behaviors. There are 3 algorithm errors, 2 miscompilations and 1 deadlock. One bug can sit in several categories.
Of 102 FlashAttention instances, 56 passed all 4 properties. The other 46 each failed a proof goal on a source bug.

Thinking Machines Lab
has released
Inkling 2 Mini
, an open-weight looped transformer with 26.4B total parameters. The model reuses its middle layers 3 times per token instead of adding more weights. That keeps the checkpoint near 20GB, small enough for a 32GB Mac or 1 NVIDIA DGX Spark. For developers, Inkling 2 Mini is a local option for agentic coding, tool use and document work. It ships under
Apache 2.0 on Hugging Face
, with hosted inference and fine-tuning on
Tinker
.
TL;DR
Size:
26.4B total, 3.4B active (5.4B effective per token with looping), up to 1M-token context.
Runs on:
Apple silicon with 32GB+ memory, 1 NVIDIA DGX Spark, or GPUs with 32GB+ VRAM. GGUF builds via Unsloth and llama.cpp.
Performance:
20.1 on the Artificial Analysis Index, tied with Qwen3.8-27B (self-reported).
Best:
79.2% on SWE-bench Verified (bash only).
Worst:
15.2% on HLE-Diamond and 50.0% on MultiChallenge.
Bottom line:
Best: strong agentic coding from a 20GB checkpoint. Worst: weaker knowledge recall and multi-turn instruction following.
What is Inkling 2 Mini?
Inkling 2 Mini is a sparse Mixture-of-Experts model from Thinking Machines that loops its middle layers. It accepts text and images and returns text only.
It follows Inkling 2 Small, a 594B-parameter model released on November 5.
How does the looped transformer work?
The model stores 24 layers, grouped into 4 blocks of 6. The first and last blocks run once. The 2 middle blocks run 3 times with shared weights. That gives 48 layer applications per token from 24 layers of weights.
Each pass after the first receives a “message” from the previous pass. Thinking Machines carries it with
Attention Residuals
and a learned gate. Feed-forward layers use 128 experts, with 8 routed per token.
Looping the middle layers gave a 1.51x to 1.91x compute-equivalent gain. Looping the last layers gave only 1.24x to 1.36x. The middle-loop variant won 27 of 28 evaluations.
Looping costs training compute but saves inference. An unlooped baseline used 7.5% less training compute. It needed 140% more inference compute to match the looped model’s loss on 512k-token agentic traces.
How was Inkling 2 Mini trained?
Training began with 384 experts per layer, with 8 active per token. At midtraining, the team pruned two-thirds of them and kept the 128 most-used experts. A 1T-token distillation run from a larger internal Inkling model then healed the pruned model. Post-training used SFT, then RL over 2.2T tokens and 2,000 steps, plus on-policy distillation.
Expert layers are trained and deployed in NVFP4. The last 4 layers use MXFP8. Thinking Machines says this removes quantization conversion loss. A research variant,
TML-d24-varloop-research
, trains with 1 to 5 passes.
How does Inkling 2 Mini perform on benchmarks?
All Inkling scores below are self-reported by Thinking Machines. Coding is the strongest area. Inkling 2 Mini scores 79.2% on SWE-bench Verified (bash only) and 77.9% on SWE-bench Pro v2 (Hard). It reaches 48.2% on DeepSWE v1.1, where
Qwen’s own card
lists Qwen3.8-27B at 42.2%. On Terminal Bench v2.1 it scores 71.6%, behind Qwen3.8-27B at 73.0%.
Agentic search also holds up: 79.0% on BrowseComp with compaction and 82.7% on MCP Atlas. For documents and vision, it posts 92.8% on OmniDocBench v1.6 and 74.9% on MMMU Pro. On reasoning, it scores 86.6% on GPQA Diamond and 49.3% on ARC-AGI-2.
Efficiency is the headline claim. On Stanford’s Intelligence per Watt metric, Thinking Machines reports 0.703 on a DGX Spark. It lists Qwen3.6-35B-A3B at 0.430 and Gemma-4-26B-A4B at 0.159.

GPT-Live-1.1 voice model
is a full-duplex model for multilingual conversations. It can listen while it speaks. OpenAI team states that it
speaks with more natural and consistent accents across languages
and completes tasks more reliably. The release also adds standby, a cheaper billing state for idle sessions. For teams running voice agents, idle time on a call now costs less. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our

TL;DR

.

v1/live/sessions

Performance:

What is GPT-Live-1.1?
GPT-Live-1.1 is a full-duplex speech model from OpenAI that hears and speaks in 1 stream. It follows
GPT-Live-1, which reached the API on September 10, 2026
. As per the
OpenAI forum announcement
, it has powered ChatGPT Plus and Pro voice since October 15.
Inputs and outputs are audio and text. Image and video are not supported. Streaming and function calling work. Structured outputs, fine-tuning and predicted outputs do not.
How does GPT-Live-1.1 work?
The GPT-Live family replaces the usual cascade of speech-to-text, an LLM and text-to-speech. OpenAI says the model
reasons over incoming and outgoing audio together in a single model
. It also handles turn detection and returns ASR transcripts natively.
Deeper work is delegated. The voice model can hand reasoning and tool calls to a backend text model. OpenAI names GPT-6 Astra for complex issues and Luna for high-volume tasks. Third-party backends also work.
The

delegation.type

client

responses

What changed from GPT-Live-1?
OpenAI lists 4 improvement areas for 1.1:
More natural and consistent accents across languages
More accurate speech transcription
Better handling of precise details like letters and numbers
More reliable instruction following and task completion

Standby pauses inference during silence while the WebRTC connection stays open.

session.wake_policy.type

speech

session.idle_timeout_s

session.wake_policy.vad_threshold
: optional, 0 to 1, default 0.5
After the timeout, the server emits
session.paused

session.resumed
fires. The session ID and history are kept. OpenAI warns the first reply after a short utterance may be slower. Keep the microphone track active during standby.
Standby works for both GPT-Live-1 and GPT-Live-1.1.

articles.summary:
Baseten released bison-1 and groundhog-1, open-weight decision models built on Gemma 4. bison-1 scores 76 on the AA Decision Index v2.1, and both models support 128k context and image input.
The post Baseten Releases Bison-1 and Groundhog-1, Topping Decision Model Index appeared first on MarkTechPost.

Baseten has released bison-1 and groundhog-1, 2 open-weight decision models built on Google’s
Gemma 4
. Decision models do not write text. They return calibrated probabilities for yes/no, choice and score questions. The Baseten bison-1 decision model scores 76 on the
Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1
. That ranks #1 of 19. Both models raise context from 16k to 128k tokens and accept images. For routing, triage and guardrail pipelines, that means full policies and histories in one call.
TL;DR
Size:
bison-1 is 31B dense. groundhog-1 is a 26B MoE with about 4B active. Both take 128k tokens (131,072).
Runs on:
Baseten Model APIs, plus open BF16 weights on Hugging Face. No inference GPU or quantized builds are listed. BF16 weights alone are about 62 GB (bison-1) and 52 GB (groundhog-1), by our arithmetic.
Performance:
bison-1 scores 76 on AA Decision Index v2.1, 1 point above Liquid AI’s d1.2-ultra (75).
Best:
When2Call, 98 (rank #1).
Worst:
AA-Omniscience-Decision v1.1, 60 (rank #11).
Bottom line:
Best: top-ranked, best-calibrated decisions (Brier 0.14) over 128k tokens at $0.10 per 1M input tokens. Worst: groundhog-1 has no official index score yet, and every number is self-reported.
What are bison-1 and groundhog-1?
bison-1 is a 31B decision model from Baseten that post-trains Gemma 4 31B to return calibrated probabilities. groundhog-1 is the cheaper sibling. It fine-tunes
Gemma 4 26B-A4B
, a mixture-of-experts model with about 4B active parameters per token.
Both join Baseten’s existing lineup: mammoth-1 (27B), elephant-1 (9B) and joey-1 (2B). Those 3 sit on Qwen backbones. The new pair is Baseten’s first on what it calls an American backbone.
How does a decision model work?
A request carries 1
state
and any number of
questions
. The state is text, optionally with images. Each question has a type:
noul
(yes/no),
choice
(named options) or
score
(ordered levels).
The model answers every question in a single prefill pass. It returns P(yes), or the chosen option with a
probabilities
field. No output tokens are generated. Baseten’s
earlier launch post
lists ticket triage, spam detection, jailbreak guardrails and LLM routing as target tasks.
Requests longer than the trained limit are refused, not truncated. Pipelines that assume silent truncation will need a length check.
Why is bison-1 better calibrated?
Baseten credits two sources: the Gemma base and more “soft labels” in the training mix. Soft labels use probability targets instead of 1 fixed correct answer. The model learns to report uncertainty that tracks how often it is right.
The result is a Brier score of 0.14, the lowest on the index. Baseten puts d1.2-ultra at 0.15. Lower is better.
How does bison-1 score on benchmarks?
On AA Decision Index v2.1, bison-1 scores 76.
Liquid AI’s d1.2-ultra
scores 75 and mammoth-1 scores 71. The index blends 6 evaluations, led by AA-Paperclip at 30%.

On long context, Baseten reports LongMemEval M (128k) of 84.8 for bison-1 and 77.4 for groundhog-1. LongMemEval S reads 87.1 and 79.3. groundhog-1 has no official index score yet. Baseten expects it to match mammoth-1.

articles.content:
Title: ClawDOS URL Source: http://ricapar.net/ClawDOS/ Final URL: https://ricapar.net/ClawDOS/ Markdown Content: ## ClawDOS **An AI coding agent for DOS.** It runs on an IBM PC XT: an 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K of RAM, a CGA card. > **A (real) human’s note:** > > > > * * * > > > **Backstory:** The IBM PC was my first computer. Rather, it was my parents’ first personal computer that I got to use at a very early age. > > > It was already obsolete by the time I was old enough to use it, but at 5 years old it was a magical device that I could make do different things depending on what I typed. > > > I learned how to type and use DOS so that I could launch some early “Learn the Alphabet” games that my mom had bought me. I learned some elementary-level use of BASIC, but at the time that didn’t progress much further than making some number guessing games and other small projects. > > > From there, many years passed but I still have some of the original parts of that PC. I have a collection of vintage machines that mean something to me, with my fully maxed-out IBM PC 5160 being the centerpiece of my collection. It still has a working 20 MB hard drive, but that’s disconnected in favor of a PicoMEM that lets me emulate a hard drive off of an SD card, making experimentation and play much easier. > > > **Old, meet new. New, meet old:** I love intersections of old and new technology. What better way to cross the two than building an AI coding agent to run on DOS on original hardware? > > > And of course, what better to build it than an AI coding agent? > > > I (read: Claude) built this for my own entertainment. I wanted to see how far I could push an AI coding agent to build something given out of the (modern) norm of constraints. Also, can that something it built then build other somethings? 100% of this repo is written by Claude, with the exception of the text within this box. > > > As explained in more detail below, the harness runs on the native OS and hardware and relies on a “bridge” PC in order to handle TLS, which would’ve been more than what an 8088 could handle. Type `CLAWDOS` at the `C:\>` prompt and talk to Claude. It reads and edits the files on your disk, writes programs, compiles them with Turbo C, runs them and looks at what they draw on the screen. It keeps notes between conversations and picks up where it left off. The whole harness runs on the PC. `HARNESS.EXE` is a 176 KB DOS program that speaks the Claude Messages API itself: it writes the requests, parses the streamed reply, runs the tools and keeps every conversation on its own disk. The 8088 does everything but TLS. ## See it work Every screen below comes from a 5160 at 4.77 MHz, emulated in 86Box. The conversations are with the live API. ### From a sentence to a running program One message: _“Write PRIMES.C: print the primes below 100. Compile it with Turbo C and run it.”_ ClawDOS reads its guide to the compilers on this machine, writes the source, then compiles, links and runs it in a single tool call. The answer is on the screen 64 seconds after Enter, 26 of them spent compiling, linking and running. The compiler gets the machine to itself. For a build, ClawDOS saves its state and leaves memory, Turbo C runs with about 450K free, and the harness comes back on the same conversation with the program’s output in hand. ### WarGames, written on the XT ClawDOS wrote this tribute to the 1983 film on the PC itself: a vector world map, missiles arcing over the pole, a tic-tac-toe endgame, and a score for the PC speaker or an AdLib card. Five files of Turbo C, 15 KB of source, a `WG.EXE` under 10 KB. Here it is running on the real 5160, filmed off its IBM monitor: ### It remembers Start a new conversation and “your WarGames demo” is all it needs. ClawDOS opens the note it saved in `C:\MEMORY`, finds the latest build, and recalls the palette trick the war scene plays on the CGA. ### It sees the screen That `Run` call asked for a screenshot 25 seconds in. A timer-interrupt hook copies the CGA’s video memory at that moment, the 8088 encodes it as a PNG, and the picture goes to Claude with the tool result. This is the file the PC made, 320x200 in four colours, 16 KB: And this is what Claude made of it: ### An agent at work Asked to make the demo exit on its own, ClawDOS goes looking. It searches the sources for the keyboard wait, reads the file, says what it found and edits one line. Each tool call shows in the transcript with its result, and between them Claude says what it is about to do. ### It plays Text art in sixteen colours, straight into the transcript, and music on the PC speaker in GW-BASIC’s `PLAY` language. ## The harness **A chat screen built for the CGA.** Replies stream onto the screen as they arrive, word-wrapped at 80 columns in code page 437. Writes are timed to the retrace, so there is no snow. The transcript scrolls in hardware through the CRTC start address, with PgUp and PgDn to go back. The spinner and its seconds run from the timer interrupt and keep moving while the PC is busy. **Eighteen tools.** Claude works on the machine through these: | Tools | What they do | | --- | --- | | `sysinfo`, `dir`, `read`, `search` | Look at the system, list directories, read files as text or hex, find text across files | | `write`, `edit`, `delete`, `mkdir`, `rename` | Create and change files; `edit` replaces one piece of a file in place | | `run` | Run DOS programs and batch files and read back what they printed, up to twelve commands in a call, with a screenshot on request | | `peek`, `poke`, `port` | Read and write memory and I/O ports | | `play`, `textart` | PC speaker music and coloured CP437 art | | `memory_list`, `memory_read`, `memory_write` | Its own notes, kept in `C:\MEMORY` | **A development kit on the disk.** Two assemblers (TINYASM and WASM), Bruce’s C, GW-BASIC and the lDebug debugger, plus Turbo C 2.0, installed from your own floppy images in `external/`. All of them are proven on the 8088, and ClawDOS knows how to drive each one. **Memories and skills.** Memories are what ClawDOS learns on your PC: what you built together, what worked, what you like. Skills are guides that ship with it, such as the dev tools and CGA demo effects. Both are plain text files on the disk, listed in every conversation’s system prompt and read when they fit the task. F4 browses the memories: **Safe mode.** On by default. Anything that changes a file, memory or a port asks `Allow ...? (y/n)` first. F3 turns it off. **Conversations that last.** Every chat is a file on the disk in the API’s own message format. F6 lists them, Enter reopens one, and your next message carries it on. A chat cut off by the power switch reopens too. **Any model, mid-conversation.**`/model` lists the providers in `CLAWDOS.CFG` and switches between them and their models without losing the conversation. F5 sets how hard Claude thinks, from low to max. Any host that speaks the Messages API works. **Easy on a slow link.** The system prompt and tools are cached by the API. After a conversation’s first request the PC uploads only what is new, so a tool result goes up in about 500 bytes. A dropped connection or an overloaded API is retried, and the turn carries on. **A flight recorder.**`CLAWDOS.LOG` has a line for every round: time to first token, upload size and time, tokens in and out, cache reads. ``` api anthropic claude-opus-5-5 round=1 ttft=2750 total=4015 up=165 len=1784 stop=tool_use in=2 out=221 cr=5543 cw=739 th=cont relaunch: program 61.5 s, CLAWDOS away 82.3 s ``` ## Under the hood ``` flowchart LR subgraph DOS["IBM PC XT (8088, 640K, CGA)"] direction TB subgraph APP["HARNESS.EXE"] direction TB UI["Chat screen"] LOOP["Agent loop
Messages API requests, SSE and JSON,
history on disk"] TOOLS["Tools
files, search, DOS programs, screenshots,
memory and ports, speaker"] end NET["mTCP + packet driver"] APP <--> NET end TUNNEL["TLS tunnel
copies bytes"] API["Claude Messages API"] NET <-->|"plain HTTP"| TUNNEL TUNNEL <-->|"HTTPS"| API ``` | | | | --- | --- | | **Machine** | IBM PC XT 5160: 8088 at 4.77 MHz, 640K, CGA. A PicoMEM card supplies the disk (an image on microSD), WiFi as an NE2000, EMS and a battery clock | | **Code** | 13,000 lines of C and C++, built with Open Watcom for the 8086 instruction set | | **Programs** | `HARNESS.EXE`, 176 KB, the whole harness. `CLAWDOS.EXE`, 29 KB, the launcher you type | | **System** | FreeDOS 1.4 with mTCP for TCP/IP | | **API** | The Claude Messages API, streamed: tool use, images, prompt caching, message threads | | **TLS** | A tunnel on another machine, `tunnel/tunnel.py`, `socat` or `stunnel`. It copies bytes between a plain port and `api.anthropic.com:443`. It can also hold the API key, so the key never touches the PC’s disk | | **Memory** | A program ClawDOS runs gets 200K beside the harness, or 450K when the harness steps out | | **Tests** | 31 boot tests in DOSBox-X against a mock API, unit tests that run on DOS, and runs on 86Box’s 8088 | [docs/API.md](https://ricapar.net/ClawDOS/docs/API.html) has exactly what ClawDOS sends and what it expects back. ## Run it You need a Mac or a Windows PC with Python 3, and an Anthropic API key. On Windows the command is `python`. ``` python3 scripts/setup-tools.py # fetch the compilers, FreeDOS, mTCP and the emulators echo ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-... > .env python3 scripts/build.py # build/CLAWDOS.IMG, a bootable disk python3 tunnel/tunnel.py # the TLS tunnel, on port 8443 python3 scripts/run86box.py # boot an IBM PC XT ``` At the `C:\>` prompt, type `CLAWDOS`. No key? `python3 tunnel/mockapi.py` plays the API offline: type `CLAWDOS 10.0.2.2:18023` and send `!help`. **On a real PC:** build with the address of the machine running the tunnel (`python3 scripts/build.py --tunnel 192.168.1.10:8443`), copy `CLAWDOS.IMG` to the PicoMEM’s microSD card, pick it as the hard disk in the PicoMEM’s menu, boot, and type `CLAWDOS`. Later builds update the card’s image in place and keep its memories and chats (`python3 scripts/build.py --update /path/to/CLAWDOS.IMG`). ## At the keyboard | Key | | | --- | --- | | Enter | Send | | Esc | Stop a reply, or clear the input | | Up / Down | Recall earlier messages | | PgUp / PgDn | Scroll back | | F1 | Help | | F2 | New chat | | F3 | Safe mode on or off | | F4 | Memories | | F5 | Effort: low, medium, high, xhigh, max | | F6 | Earlier chats | | F10 | Quit | `/model`, `/chats`, `/memories`, `/new` and `/quit` work from the input box. `CLAWDOS -m "..."` sends a message from the command line and `-c NAME` reopens a chat. ## More | | | | --- | --- | | [docs/MANUAL.md](https://ricapar.net/ClawDOS/docs/MANUAL.html) | Setup in full, real hardware, the image updater, other providers, every setting | | [docs/API.md](https://ricapar.net/ClawDOS/docs/API.html) | What ClawDOS sends to the API and expects back | | [docs/ROADMAP.md](https://ricapar.net/ClawDOS/docs/ROADMAP.html) | The plan, the benchmark and the memory map | | Path | What | | --- | --- | | `src/harness/` | HARNESS.EXE: the chat screen, the turn, the tools | | `src/clawdos/` | CLAWDOS.EXE, the launcher | | `lib/` | The pieces: screen, console, network and HTTP, the API request writer and stream parser, JSON, history, the tool executors, screenshots and the PNG encoder | | `tunnel/` | The TLS tunnel and the mock Messages API | | `image/` | What goes on the disk: the manifest, the system prompt, the tool schemas, the skills, the tests | | `scripts/` | Build, disk image tools, the emulator runners and test harnesses | | `tests/unit/` | DOSUNIT.EXE, the unit tests that run on DOS | ## License ClawDOS is free software under the GNU General Public License, version 3 or (at your option) any later version: see [LICENSE](https://github.com/Ricapar/ClawDO

Title: These surprisingly adorable insect portraits reveal an astonishing hidden world you never knew existed

URL Source: https://amateurphotographer.com/latest/these-astonishing-insect-portraits-reveal-a-hidden-world-you-never-knew-existed/

Published Time: 2026-11-20T11:45:00+00:00

Markdown Content:
Daro Ojo’s new book is crammed full of tiny creatures with bulging eyes, elaborate armour, extraordinary colours and faces that look as though they’ve smashed through the screen of a science-fiction film. They are more than just fascinating subjects, they are crucial to the survival of our planet.

Tiny Titans: The Silent Keepers of Our Ecosystem, by [macro photographer](https://amateurphotographer.com/buying-advice/the-best-cameras-for-photography/) and conservation storyteller Dara Ojo introduces us to the often-overlooked inhabitants of our natural world through a collection of remarkable and detailed portraits. A spider with enormous eyes stares directly into the lens. Droplets of dew that look like minuscule glass beads cover an insect. A moth resembles an intricately embroidered piece of fabric. Across 288 pages Ojo’s camera captures behaviour on a scale rarely experienced by the naked eye, transforming insects, spiders and other arthropods into captivating characters. They are intricate and deliver an unexpected beauty alongside curious behaviour.

It’s tempting to anthropomorphise some of them. Several appear positively camera-ready, while others have expressions that suggest they’ve just discovered something rather unpleasant in their inbox. The visual entertainment is underpinned by a serious message. Small doesn’t mean insignificant and these tiny creatures are among the most important labourers on the planet. They pollinate plants, recycle nutrients, build soils, control pests and support the food chains on which countless other species, including us, depend.

### Close beginnings

The origins of Ojo’s photographic ambition wasn’t grand, beginning during the Covid-a9 pandemic, when he was living in China. The travel restrictions and slower pace to everyday life allowed him time to learn photography properly. He’d experimented photographing birds but became increasingly interested in macro photography after a friend mentioned the technique. He purchased a Tamron 90mm macro lens and constructed a makeshift flash diffuser using a Pringles can and paper towel. His first attempt was memorable for the wrong reasons. Heading out at two in the afternoon to photograph dragonflies in harsh sunlight, he returned sweaty, frustrated and ready to give up.

Ojo persevered and what developed was an obsession with the miniature world that surrounded him. Public parks, garden borders and tree bark all became adventure playgrounds for his photography. What crystalised in Ojo’s mind was that macro photography was about more than getting close – it demanded patience, stillness and a willingness to wait until his subjects stopped reacting to his presence and resumed their natural behaviour.

### A world beneath our feet

Ojo has refined his approach to appreciate the humour, drama, and at times, introduce an unexpected tenderness to these astonishing encounters. A flower mantis appears almost sculptural. A longhorn beetle’s face is revealed in extraordinary detail, droplets of dew rest in its eyes. A net-casting ogre-faced spider holds its folded hunting net between its front legs, ready to catch unsuspecting prey. A group of newly hatched stink-bug nymphs forms a perfect circle around their empty eggshells. A green jumping spider is documented constructing its tiny retreat across a sequence of photographs.

Each location brought different challenges and discoveries. The book follows Ojo’s photographic journey across China, Costa Rica, Canada, Mexico and Nigeria. The abundance of rainforest life provided an extraordinary variety of subjects in Costa Rica. He negotiated slippery trails during a 16-day stay in a conservation forest in Tinamaste discovering creatures that seemed otherworldly. Mexico offered a brief encounter with desert adapted-species.

### Returning home

Nigeria delivered smoothing more personal. Ojo grew up in Lagos, where his early experiences of nature including farming with his father, helped shape his interest in the natural world. Following his father’s death in 2025, Ojo returned and began exploring familiar surroundings through a macro lens. He was discovering an entirely new world beneath the feet that had walked Nigerian streets for 25 years. A classic reminder that sometimes you have to leave home to learn how to see it afresh.

Now based in Edmonton, Canada, the country offers a different perspective. Six months of cold and six months of warmth shape the natural environment. Ojo’s photographic routine has adapted and became somewhat extreme with 3am starts and late-night visits to botanical gardens. Cooler morning temperatures presented perfect conditions, slowing insect movement where dew settled across wings and bodies.

### Small creatures, big responsibility

Technically, the photographs are as impressive. Ojo explains in an appendix that all the images were made outdoors, in natural conditions and on location. Most of his photographs were taken before sunrise or late at night, using low-powered flash and diffusers. Focus bracketing allowed multiple frames at slightly different focus distances before being combined to create images with exceptional depth of field. The colourful backgrounds are created in camera using physical colour cards or naturally occurring elements. The droplets of water and dew aren’t added. In an age when it’s easy to digitally manipulate nature photography it’s important to be clear how images are made.

Canadian naturalist and television personality John Acorn provides the book’s foreword. In it he describes how Ojo’s portraits encourage us to look into the eyes of creatures we might otherwise dismiss. Welcome contributions are also made by scientists and naturalists, who provide short explanations of the species and their ecological roles alongside the photographs.

### Rocky mountain books

Arthropods are frequently feared, swatted or overlooked, despite their fundamental contribution to functioning ecosystems. Conservation is central to Ojo’s project, his intention isn’t simply to make them look beautiful, but to encourage a greater appreciation of their existence and the delicate relationships that sustain life.

You don’t need to be an entomologist, conservationist or even fond of insects to appreciate the photographs in Tiny Titans. Its success lies in its ability to make an unfamiliar world feel gloriously alive and accessible. It makes you curious and care enough that having turned the final page, you might hesitate to reach for the swatter the next time an insect crawls or flaps into your space.

Tiny Titans: The Silent Keepers of Our Ecosystem by Dara Ojo, with a foreword by John Acorn, is published by Rocky Mountain Books. Available in hardcover and Kindle editions – explorewithdara.com @explorewithdara

Title: Pandex: Europe's law, in one API.

URL Source: https://www.pandex.io/

Markdown Content:
Legislation and highest-court decisions of the EU and seven European countries, straight from the institutions that publish them, ready for search and AI agents.

2.8M official documents

33 of 41 institutions held complete

37M citations linked to their text

Works with the AI tools you already use.

*   Claude
*   Cursor
*   GitHub Copilot
*   Windsurf
*   Zed
*   Gemini

## Built for software that has to get the law right.

One API and one MCP server for every jurisdiction we hold.

REST API MCP server Markdown or JSON

Keyword, semantic or hybrid search in any language. Ask in English, find the French ruling and the passage that answers it.

Is a bike courier working for a delivery app an employee?

France Case law 28 Nov 2018

Cour de cassation, chambre sociale, 28 novembre 2018, n° 17-20.079

> … le lien de subordinationest caractérisé par l'exécution d'un travail sous l'autorité d'un employeur qui a le pouvoir de donner des ordres et des directives …

## Built for teams that work with the law.

*
*
*

*   ### Legal AI and agents

Ground every answer in real law, with citations. Connect over MCP or the API.
*   ### Compliance and monitoring

Follow every change to the law across jurisdictions: each article with its past versions and the date each one took effect.
*   ### Legal research products

One API and one schema across countries, instead of a scraper for every court.

## Coverage you can check, straight from the source.

National legislation with its past versions and the decisions of the highest courts, institution by institution. We publish what we hold of each one, and what we do not.

Court decisions 2.4M

Acts and codes 421K

Searchable passages 112M

Linked citations 37M

Institutions complete 33/41

907,232 documents

177,101 documents

    *   Centrale Raad van Beroep complete

99,621 documents

137,746 documents

41,891 documents

The older judgments are only behind the search of justice.public.lu, which asks for a proof-of-work challenge.

    *   Cour administrative complete

    *   Cour constitutionnelle complete

127,432 documents

A key is free and takes a minute. For more than that, tell us what you’re building.
